Chapter 23

Async Svelte, and its sharp edges

await inside $derived, the boundary SvelteKit already wrote, boundaries of your own, and two traps that cost this project an afternoon each.

By the end of this chapter

Components that await data directly, with sensible loading and error states — and no server-side crashes.

Svelte 5 with experimental.async lets you await inside $derived and directly in markup. It removes an entire category of code: no {#await} pyramids, no loading booleans, no data.streamed.thing.

Boundaries, and the one SvelteKit already wrote

An awaiting component needs somewhere for its loading and error states to live. That is <svelte:boundary>: an await that has not settled suspends the nearest boundary above it, and a promise that rejects puts that boundary into its failed state.

In a SvelteKit 3 app you do not write the outermost one. SvelteKit renders everything below the root layout inside a boundary of its own, and that boundary's failed state is the nearest +error.svelte. So the app-wide failure screen is a file, not a snippet:

error is an App.Error: { status, message }, plus the id this app declares in app.d.ts. It has already been through handleError (the server's, or the browser's for a bug that throws there), so message is either the sentence somebody wrote in error(…) or the hook's safe replacement, and the component shows it as it is. The id appears only for unknown failures, the ones the hook logged next to a stack trace. The heading is chosen from the status, because a 403 is the server refusing on purpose, and "Something went wrong" would tell somebody the app is broken when it is working exactly as designed.

Why error.message, and not messageFrom

Chapter 20's helper is for a catch around a remote call, which receives an HttpError with the words one level down, in body. A boundary receives the App.Error itself, with no body, because SvelteKit has already unwrapped it. Hand that to messageFrom and the fallback wins every time, while a plausible sentence sits on screen and nothing looks broken. We probed it rather than trusting it: on the server and after a client-side navigation alike, the failed state was handed a plain object, { status: 404, message: 'We could not find that booking.' }, neither an Error nor an HttpError.

That comment is a confession. This layout used to wrap children in a boundary of its own, with a failed snippet showing a "Something went wrong" card and a Try again button. It looked like the app's error handling, and it could never run: SvelteKit's boundary sits between the layout and the page and catches every error first. What visitors actually got was SvelteKit's bare default page, a status code above a sentence. The card hid a second bug behind the first, too. It passed error to messageFrom, so had it ever rendered, it would have shown the fallback.

Two tests for one screen, because there are two roads to it. A fresh load renders the failure on the server. Following a link renders it in the browser, where the query's rejection arrives over the network and SvelteKit unwraps it into an App.Error before the boundary sees it. arriveClientSide, in e2e/fixtures.ts, gets there by clicking a link inside the running app and then checks that no page load happened on the way, so the second test cannot quietly turn into the first. Both fail against the old layout, which had no alert to find, and both fail if +error.svelte is changed to read messageFrom(error, …); we made each change and watched.

A boundary of your own

Write <svelte:boundary> yourself when one region of a page can fail on its own while the rest stays useful: a chart, a feed, a panel of suggestions. Its failed snippet receives the same App.Error as +error.svelte, because SvelteKit passes every boundary's error through handleError on its way in, and so does onerror. The SvelteKit documentation shows the shape:

The snippet takes a second argument, reset, which throws the failed content away and renders it afresh: the Try again button. A probe page with a boundary around an awaited query that rejects showed the same { status: 404, message: 'We could not find that booking.' } in both failed and onerror, on a fresh load and after a client-side navigation.

A boundary only catches what renders inside it. An await in a component's <script> suspends the boundary above that component, so a boundary in the same component's markup never sees it. Put the await in the markup inside the boundary, or move the region into a child component. Every page in this app awaits in its script, which is exactly why its failures belong to +error.svelte.

Trap one: pending on the server

A pending snippet renders immediately during server rendering and does not wait for the awaits. Put one on a boundary that wraps a whole page and every page in your app ships HTML whose entire body is the word "Loading…". The page looks fine in a browser — it hydrates a moment later — and is empty to a search engine, a link preview, and anybody on a slow connection. We shipped that for an hour before noticing.

The fix is to put pending only where a client-side wait is genuinely expected — a panel that refetches when a filter changes — and never on the boundary that wraps a whole page.

Trap two: declaration order with bound state

When a component binds to a member of a $state object — bind:value={draft.weekday} — the compiler emits a getter that runs before the part of the script following the first awaited $derived. Declare the state after those and it is still undefined when the getter runs. Server rendering dies with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'weekday')" and the page 500s before anybody sees it.

Move let draft above the $derived and it renders. Binding to a plain $state variable is unaffected, and so is reading draft.weekday in ordinary markup — which is exactly what makes it so easy to walk into, and so confusing when it happens.

The rule to remember: declare any state you bind: to at the top of the script, above anything that awaits. It costs nothing, and it is a good habit regardless.

Effects that trigger themselves

One more, because it produces a symptom that makes no sense — radio buttons that will not stay selected — and because the real fix turned out to be deleting the code.

The booking page used to forget the chosen time whenever the service, the person or the day changed, because a time picked for one of those means nothing for another. The obvious effect for that:

The first fix was untrack, which says "run this, but do not count what it reads as a dependency". Wrapped in it, the set no longer subscribed the effect to the field, and the three void lines were left as the only things that re-ran it:

It worked, and it was still the wrong shape. A second effect beside it cleared the field again when the live grid dropped the chosen time. Both were state written in reaction to other state, which is the one job the Svelte docs tell you not to give an effect: "Effects are an escape hatch and should mostly be avoided. In particular, avoid updating state inside effects." What the page actually needed to know was not "has something changed since the time was picked" but "is the picked time on screen right now" — and that is a value you can derive.

selected is the chosen slot if it is one of the times on screen, and null otherwise. Look at another day, narrow to another person, or lose the time to somebody else, and it becomes null — no effect, no untrack, no clearing — and the summary, the time-zone note and the details form all follow it. Nothing writes state in response to anything, so nothing can wake itself up.

When untrack is still the answer

untrack is not a smell; an effect writing state is. Keep it for an effect with a genuine side effect — talking to a library, the DOM, the network — that has to read something without subscribing to it. If the thing you are writing could be a $derived instead, make it one, and the trap disappears along with the effect.

Why this is worth the sharp edges

In SvelteKit 2, data that arrived late came from a load function that returned a promise without awaiting it, and the page unwrapped it with {#await}. Even with runes, every component that wanted the value wrote its own three states:

The loading and error states did not disappear — they moved to a boundary, where they are written once for a whole region instead of once per await. Multiply that across a dozen components and it is a different codebase. (TimesList is a stand-in for any component that takes the data, not a file in this project; the real slot grid takes one day's slots, a zone and a form field.)

Checkpoint

Every page in the app server-renders its real content — view source and see the studio name, not "Loading…". Then open /booking/ZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZ, once by typing it and once by following a link to it from inside the app: both times you get your own failure screen, headed "Not found", saying "We could not find that booking."
